F22.quote: Researchers from MIT, Cohere for AI, and 11 other institutions launch free Data Provenance Explorer platform to track and filter audited datasets for ethical, legal, and transparency considerations
F22.claim: the launch: MIT, Cohere for AI and 11 other institutions release the free Explorer to track and filter audited datasets
F22.lineage: origin: the founding audit and the launch, October 2023

F23.quote: Inconsistent tracking of the origins of a piece of data, which we refer to as data provenance, has introduced a range of legal and ethical challenges.
F23.claim: data provenance defined by the authors: the tracking of the origins of a piece of data; its inconsistency raises legal and ethical challenges

F24.quote: audit and trace nearly 2,000 of the most widely used fine-tuning datasets. Collectively, these data sets have been downloaded tens of millions of times, and are the backbone of many published NLP breakthroughs.
F24.claim: the founding audit as the launch states it: nearly 2,000 widely used fine-tuning datasets, downloaded tens of millions of times
F24.lineage: origin: the founding audit and the launch, October 2023

F25.quote: The result of this multidisciplinary initiative is the single largest audit to date of AI datasets. For the first time, these datasets include tags to the original data sources, numerous re-licensings, creators, and other data properties.
F25.claim: the largest audit of AI datasets to date; the datasets tagged with original sources, re-licensings and creators
F25.lineage: the unit: a dataset traced to its sources, licences and creators

F26.quote: The platform allows developers to track and filter thousands of datasets for legal and ethical considerations, and enables scholars and journalists to explore the composition and data lineage of popular AI datasets.
F26.claim: the platform's users: developers filtering for legal and ethical considerations; scholars and journalists exploring composition and data lineage
F26.lineage: what it is: the explorer of an audit of training datasets

F27.quote: Crowdsourced aggregators like GitHub, Papers with Code, and many of the open source LLMs trained from data on these aggregators, have an extremely high proportion of missing data licenses (“Unspecified”), ranging from 72 to 83 percent. This compares to 30 percent missing licenses with our own annotation protocol
F27.claim: crowdsourced aggregators (GitHub, Papers with Code) miss licences for 72–83 percent of datasets, against 30 percent under the Initiative's protocol
F27.lineage: audit findings: licence omission and misattribution

F28.quote: Crowdsourced aggregators listed licenses too permissively in up to 29 percent of the various cases audited. Incorrect or distorted licensing leads to cascading misattribution
F28.claim: aggregators list licences too permissively in up to 29 percent of cases; distorted licensing cascades into misattribution
F28.lineage: audit findings: licence omission and misattribution

F29.quote: There is a sharp and widening divide between data licensed as commercially open versus closed.
F29.claim: a widening divide between commercially open and closed data
F29.lineage: audit findings: the commercial divide and the Western skew

F30.quote: We find a stark Western-centric skew in representation across datasets.
F30.claim: a Western-centric skew in the datasets' geographic coverage
F30.lineage: audit findings: the commercial divide and the Western skew

F31.quote: major legal ambiguities remain in data licensing that the authors acknowledge cannot be resolved by tooling alone.
F31.claim: the stated limit: legal ambiguities in data licensing that tooling alone cannot resolve
F31.lineage: stated limits: what tooling cannot resolve

F32.quote: This large-scale audit is the launch of a wider multi-institutional initiative, where users all over the world can contribute to the explorer
F32.claim: the audit launches a wider initiative; users can contribute to the explorer
F32.lineage: origin: the founding audit and the launch, October 2023

F33.quote: [Submitted on 25 Oct 2023 (v1), last revised 4 Nov 2023 (this version, v3)] … Title:The Data Provenance Initiative: A Large Scale Audit of Dataset Licensing & Attribution in AI … Authors:Shayne Longpre, Robert Mahari, Anthony Chen, Naana Obeng-Marnu
F33.claim: the founding paper, submitted 25 October 2023 (v3 4 November), by Longpre, Mahari, Chen, Obeng-Marnu and others
F33.lineage: origin: the founding audit and the launch, October 2023

F34.quote: we convene a multi-disciplinary effort between legal and machine learning experts to systematically audit and trace 1800+ text datasets. We develop tools and standards to trace the lineage of these datasets, from their source, creators, series of license conditions, properties, and subsequent use.
F34.claim: the founding audit: 1800+ text datasets traced by legal and ML experts from source and creators through licence conditions to subsequent use
F34.lineage: origin: the founding audit and the launch, October 2023

F35.quote: Our landscape analysis highlights the sharp divides in composition and focus of commercially open vs closed datasets, with closed datasets monopolizing important categories: lower resource languages, more creative tasks, richer topic variety, newer and more synthetic training data.
F35.claim: closed datasets monopolize lower-resource languages, creative tasks, topic variety and newer synthetic data
F35.lineage: audit findings: the commercial divide and the Western skew

F36.quote: We also observe frequent miscategorization of licenses on widely used dataset hosting sites, with license omission of 70%+ and error rates of 50%+. This points to a crisis in misattribution and informed use of the most popular datasets driving many recent breakthroughs.
F36.claim: on hosting sites, licence omission of 70%+ and error rates of 50%+: a crisis in misattribution
F36.lineage: audit findings: licence omission and misattribution

F37.quote: we release our entire audit, with an interactive UI, the Data Provenance Explorer, which allows practitioners to trace and filter on data provenance for the most popular open source finetuning data collections
F37.claim: the Explorer defined by the paper: the whole audit released with an interactive UI to trace and filter on provenance of popular open fine-tuning collections
F37.lineage: what it is: the explorer of an audit of training datasets

F38.quote: [Submitted on 20 Jul 2024 (v1), last revised 24 Jul 2024 (this version, v2)] … Title:Consent in Crisis: The Rapid Decline of the AI Data Commons … Authors:Shayne Longpre, Robert Mahari, Ariel Lee
F38.claim: Consent in Crisis, submitted 20 July 2024, by Longpre, Mahari, Lee and others
F38.lineage: the Web Data Explorer and Consent in Crisis

F39.quote: we conduct the first, large-scale, longitudinal audit of the consent protocols for the web domains underlying AI training corpora. Our audit of 14,000 web domains provides an expansive view of crawlable web data and how codified data use preferences are changing over time.
F39.claim: the second audit: the first longitudinal audit of consent protocols for 14,000 web domains underlying AI training corpora
F39.lineage: the Web Data Explorer and Consent in Crisis

F40.quote: in a single year (2023-2024) there has been a rapid crescendo of data restrictions from web sources, rendering ~5%+ of all tokens in C4, or 28%+ of the most actively maintained, critical sources in C4, fully restricted from use. For Terms of Service crawling restrictions, a full 45% of C4 is now restricted.
F40.claim: in one year ~5%+ of C4's tokens (28%+ of its critical sources) fully restricted; by terms of service, 45% of C4
F40.lineage: consent findings: the decline of the AI data commons

F41.quote: We diagnose these as symptoms of ineffective web protocols, not designed to cope with the widespread re-purposing of the internet for AI.
F41.claim: the restrictions diagnosed as symptoms of web protocols not designed for AI's re-purposing of the internet
F41.lineage: consent findings: the decline of the AI data commons

F42.quote: If respected or enforced, these restrictions are rapidly biasing the diversity, freshness, and scaling laws for general-purpose AI systems.
F42.claim: conditional: if respected or enforced, the restrictions bias diversity, freshness and scaling laws
F42.lineage: consent findings: the decline of the AI data commons
